title: Freemasons and the American Founding
bigQuestion: Which founders were really Masons, and how can the paper trail test a popular claim?

story.title: The Eye on the Dollar
story.kicker: A student holds up a one-dollar bill and asks a question that takes the whole class back to 1776.
paragraphs: It is a gray Tuesday in a middle school classroom. The lesson is about the American Revolution. Maya raises her hand. She is holding a one-dollar bill she found in her backpack. She turns it over and points to the back.

"Who put that eye on top of the pyramid?" she asks. "My cousin says the Freemasons did. He says they secretly designed the whole country." A few students lean in. The eye does look mysterious. It floats inside a glowing triangle above a pyramid with no top.

Her teacher smiles. "That is a great question," he says. "Lots of people have heard that story. So let's test it. Who designed that picture? When? Were they Masons? What papers do we have from the time?" He writes three words on the board: Who. When. Proof.

Over the next few days, the class follows a trail of old papers. There is a committee report from 1776. There is a vote in Congress from 1782. There are letters written by two founders in 1798. And there is a decision about the dollar made in 1935. Each paper adds a piece. By the end, Maya can answer her own question, with evidence.
story.think: Before you read the chapter, what would you need to see to believe that Masons designed the eye on the dollar?

lessons.title: Franklin, Printer and Mason
lessons.mainIdea: Benjamin Franklin joined a Philadelphia lodge in 1731 and became a leading Mason and a printer of Masonic books.
reading: In 1730, Benjamin Franklin was a young printer in Philadelphia. He owned a newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. In December 1730 his paper reported that several lodges of Freemasons had been set up in the colony. People were curious and guessing about them. Franklin's tone was a bit teasing.

A few months later, Franklin joined one of those lodges himself. He became a member of St. John's Lodge in Philadelphia in 1731. By 1734 he was *Grand Master* of the Masons of Pennsylvania, the leader of all the lodges there.

That same year, Franklin used his press to reprint Anderson's Constitutions. It was the first Masonic book printed in America. Later, while he lived in France, Franklin belonged to a famous Paris lodge called the Nine Sisters.
Franklin's story shows how a *fraternity*, a brotherhood club, could spread through print. A rulebook from London crossed the ocean and was sold in Philadelphia by a printer who was also a member.

words.d: the elected leader of all the lodges in one area
a club or brotherhood of men who share rules and goals

look.title: From Joke to Member
look.text: December 1730: Franklin's newspaper tells readers that people have been busy guessing about the new lodges in the colony. 1731: Franklin joins St. John's Lodge. 1734: Franklin is Grand Master of Pennsylvania and prints the Masons' rulebook.
look.prompt: How did Franklin's view of the lodges seem to change in four years? What might explain the change?

check.q: Which lodge did Franklin join in 1731?
choices: The Goose and Gridiron in London
check.why: The reading says Franklin became a member of St. John's Lodge in Philadelphia in 1731.

check.q: What did Franklin print in 1734?
choices: Anderson's Constitutions, the first Masonic book printed in America
check.why: The reading says Franklin reprinted Anderson's Constitutions in 1734, the first Masonic book printed in America.

check.q: What is a fraternity?
choices: A club or brotherhood of men who share rules and goals
A tax paid to a king
check.why: The reading defines a fraternity as a brotherhood club.

lessons.title: Young Washington Joins
lessons.mainIdea: George Washington joined a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, in 1752, when he was 20 years old.
reading: On 4 November 1752, a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, wrote a short note in its account book. It said that Mr. George Washington had been made an Entered Apprentice that evening. Washington was 20 years old. He paid a fee of two pounds and three shillings.

A *ledger* is a book where money and events are recorded. The lodge's ledger shows each step Washington took. He became a Fellow Craft on 3 March 1753 and a Master Mason on 4 August 1753. That is less than a year for all three degrees.
Washington stayed a Mason all his life. In 1788 he was named master of the lodge in Alexandria, Virginia, near his home at Mount Vernon. When he died in 1799, Masons took part in his funeral.
Some later stories made Washington the head of all American Masons. That is not true. No such office existed. The records show a real member, but not a national leader of the fraternity.

words.d: a book where money paid and received, and other events, are written down
the first degree, or step, of a new Mason

look.title: The Lodge Ledger, 1752
look.text: On 4 November 1752, the lodge treasurer writes that on this evening Mr. George Washington was made an Entered Apprentice, and records the fee he paid.
look.cite: Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4, ledger entry, 4 November 1752, as transcribed by the Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why is an account book written that same evening strong evidence that Washington joined?

check.q: Where did George Washington join a lodge in 1752?
check.why: The reading says a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, recorded Washington joining on 4 November 1752.

check.q: What is a ledger?
choices: A book where money and events are recorded
check.why: The reading defines a ledger as a book where money and events are recorded.

check.q: Which claim about Washington does the reading say is NOT true?
choices: He joined a lodge at age 20
He became a Master Mason in 1753
He was named master of a lodge in 1788
He was head of all American Masons
check.why: The reading says no national head of Masons existed, so the claim that Washington led all American Masons is false.

lessons.title: Boston's Patriot Masons
lessons.mainIdea: Several Boston patriots, including Paul Revere and Joseph Warren, were active Masons.
reading: Paul Revere was a silversmith in Boston. He made cups, spoons and engraved prints. Today he is famous for his midnight ride in April 1775, warning that British troops were coming. He was also a devoted Mason.
Revere belonged to St. Andrew's Lodge in Boston. He stayed active for decades. In the 1790s he served as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, the top leader of the state's Masons.

Another member was Dr. Joseph Warren, a Boston doctor and patriot leader. Warren led a group of Massachusetts Masons before the war. He was killed at the Battle of Bunker Hill in June 1775. John Hancock, who signed the Declaration of Independence first, was also a Mason.

So some well-known patriots were Masons. That is *documented*, which means proved by records from the time. But being in the same club does not prove the club planned the Revolution. Many patriots were not Masons, and many Masons were not patriots.

words.d: proved by records made at the time, such as ledgers, letters or minutes
in the American Revolution, a colonist who supported independence from Britain

look.title: Same Club, Same Plan?
look.text: Three players on a soccer team are also in the school band. The band wins a contest. A student says: the soccer team must have planned the band's win. Another student says: they are in both groups, but that does not show one group planned what the other did.
look.prompt: How is this like the claim that Masons planned the Revolution because some patriots were Masons?

check.q: What leadership role did Paul Revere hold in the 1790s?
choices: Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
check.why: The reading says Revere served as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in the 1790s.

check.q: Which patriot Mason was killed at Bunker Hill in 1775?
check.why: The reading says Dr. Joseph Warren, a leader of Massachusetts Masons, was killed at Bunker Hill in June 1775.

check.q: Why does the reading say the club did not necessarily plan the Revolution?
choices: Many patriots were not Masons, and many Masons were not patriots
Masons were not allowed in Boston
The Revolution happened before lodges existed
check.why: The reading says belonging to the same club does not prove a plan, since the groups only partly overlapped.

lessons.title: John Adams Says No
lessons.mainIdea: In 1798 John Adams wrote to Massachusetts Masons that he had never been made a Mason.
reading: In 1798, John Adams was President of the United States. The country was worried about a possible war with France. The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts sent him a friendly letter of support. Its Grand Master was Josiah Bartlett.

On 22 June 1798, Adams wrote back. He thanked the Masons warmly. Then he said something plain. He had never had the chance to be initiated into their fraternity. To be *initiated* means to be brought into a group through a ceremony.

Adams also praised the Masons he had known. He said many of his best friends were Masons. So the letter is friendly, not angry. It does not attack the lodge at all. It simply shows that he was not a member.
This is a strong kind of evidence. It is a *firsthand* statement, from the person himself, written at the time. Anyone who says Adams was a Mason has to explain away his own letter.

words.d: brought into a group through a special ceremony
coming directly from the person who saw or did something

look.title: Adams Writes to the Grand Lodge, 1798
look.text: Adams tells the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts that he has never had the honor of belonging to their ancient fraternity and has never been initiated. He adds that many of the friends he has valued most were Masons.
look.cite: John Adams to Josiah Bartlett and the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, 22 June 1798, Founders Online, National Archives (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What two things does Adams say in this letter? Why is it hard to argue that he was secretly a Mason?

check.q: What did John Adams tell the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1798?
choices: He was their new Grand Master
He had never been initiated as a Mason
check.why: In his letter of 22 June 1798, Adams wrote that he had never been initiated into their fraternity.

check.q: What was the tone of Adams's letter?
choices: Friendly, praising Masons he had known
check.why: The reading says Adams thanked the Masons warmly and praised Masons he had known.

check.q: Why is Adams's letter a firsthand source?
choices: It was written by a historian in 1950
It was carved on a monument
It comes directly from Adams himself, written at the time
It was a rumor told by neighbors
check.why: Firsthand means coming directly from the person, and Adams wrote the letter himself in 1798.

lessons.title: Jefferson and the Missing Record
lessons.mainIdea: No record shows that Thomas Jefferson was a Mason, so careful historians say he is not known to have been one.
reading: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence. Later he became the third president. Many websites, posters and lists of famous Masons include his name. Is that true? Let's check the records.

Historians have looked for lodge records with his name. They have found none. Monticello, the museum at Jefferson's home, says he is not known to have belonged to any fraternal group such as the Freemasons. No lodge list, minute or letter names him as a member.

Notice the careful wording: "not known to have belonged." Historians rarely say "never" unless they have a statement like Adams's letter. With Jefferson, we have an *absence of evidence*, meaning no records turn up. That is different from proof that something never happened.

So the honest answer is this. We have no evidence that Jefferson was a Mason. Until someone finds a real record, a claim that he was one is *unsupported*. A lodge list, a letter or a minute could change that answer.

words.d: when no records or proof can be found for a claim
describes a claim that has no good evidence behind it

look.title: Three Ways to Say It
look.text: Statement 1: Jefferson was a Freemason. Statement 2: Jefferson was never a Freemason, and he said so. Statement 3: Jefferson is not known to have been a Freemason; no lodge record of him has been found.
look.prompt: Which statement best matches the evidence in this lesson? What is wrong with each of the other two?

check.q: What does Monticello say about Jefferson and the Freemasons?
choices: He was Grand Master of Virginia
He joined in Paris with Franklin
He is not known to have belonged to any such group
check.why: The reading says Monticello states he is not known to have belonged to any fraternal group such as the Freemasons.

check.q: How is the evidence about Jefferson different from the evidence about Adams?
choices: Jefferson wrote a letter saying he was a Mason
For Jefferson, no record is found; Adams wrote that he was not a Mason
Adams has lodge records; Jefferson does not
check.why: Adams gave a firsthand statement, while for Jefferson there is only an absence of evidence.

check.q: What does absence of evidence mean?
choices: No records or proof can be found for a claim
A secret record kept by a lodge
A letter that was lost at sea
check.why: The reading defines absence of evidence as no records turning up, which is different from proof that something never happened.

lessons.title: How Often Washington Went
lessons.mainIdea: In letters of 1798, Washington said he rarely attended a lodge and believed American lodges were not part of any plot.
reading: In 1798, many Americans were afraid of a secret group called the Illuminati. It had been started in Bavaria, in Germany, in 1776 and was shut down there in the 1780s. Books claimed it was secretly working through Masonic lodges.
A man named G. W. Snyder sent Washington one of these books. He worried that American lodges were in danger. Washington answered him in two letters, on 25 September and 24 October 1798.

Washington wrote that he did not lead any lodge. He said he had seldom been inside one in many years. He also said he did not believe any lodges in this country were spreading Illuminati ideas. He did think such ideas might be spreading in other ways.
These letters are useful. Washington was a real Mason, but in old age he said his part in lodge life had been small. Letters like these help us measure a claim, not just repeat it.

words.d: a secret society founded in Bavaria in 1776 and shut down in the 1780s
a statement that something is true, which may or may not have evidence

look.title: Washington Answers a Worried Writer
look.text: Washington tells Snyder that he presides over no lodge and has rarely been in one for many years. He adds that he does not believe any of the lodges in this country hold the ideas blamed on the Illuminati.
look.cite: George Washington to G. W. Snyder, 25 September 1798, George Washington Papers, Library of Congress (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What does this letter tell you about how active Washington was in his lodge late in life?

check.q: Why did G. W. Snyder write to Washington in 1798?
choices: He wanted Washington to join a lodge
He asked Washington to design a seal
He worried that the Illuminati were working through lodges
He wanted to buy land at Mount Vernon
check.why: The reading says Snyder sent Washington a book claiming the Illuminati worked through lodges and worried about it.

check.q: What did Washington say about his own lodge life?
choices: He attended a lodge every week
He led no lodge and had seldom attended one in many years

check.why: Washington wrote that he did not lead any lodge and had seldom been in one for many years.

check.q: What did Washington believe about American lodges?
choices: All of them were run by the Illuminati

None of them were spreading Illuminati ideas
check.why: Washington wrote that he did not believe any lodges in this country held Illuminati ideas.

lessons.title: The Capitol Cornerstone, 1793
lessons.mainIdea: On 18 September 1793, Washington helped lay the cornerstone of the U.S. Capitol in a public Masonic ceremony.
reading: A *cornerstone* is the first stone set at the corner of a new building. In the 1700s, laying it was a big public event. Masons often led these ceremonies. It made sense, since their fraternity took its symbols from builders.

On 18 September 1793, a crowd gathered on a hill in the new federal city, which would become Washington, D.C. The Grand Lodge of Maryland led the ceremony, with members of Alexandria Lodge No. 22 from Virginia. President Washington took part as a Mason.
Washington laid a silver plate with the stone. It recorded the date and the event. There was a parade, music and speeches. It was one of the most public things the Masons did in the young nation.
Here is a surprise. Today no one knows exactly where that cornerstone is. Searches have not found it. The ceremony is well documented, but the stone itself is hidden somewhere in the Capitol's walls.

words.d: the first stone set at a corner of a new building, often in a ceremony
a formal event done in a set way to mark something important

look.title: Washington's Masonic Life in Years
look.cite: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, Freemasonry; U.S. Senate, Washington Lays Capitol Cornerstone
look.prompt: How old was Washington, born in 1732, when he laid the Capitol cornerstone? How many years passed between joining and the cornerstone?

check.why: The reading says the ceremony took place on 18 September 1793.

check.q: Which Grand Lodge led the Capitol ceremony?
check.why: The reading says the Grand Lodge of Maryland led the ceremony, with Alexandria Lodge No. 22.

check.q: Why did Masons often lead cornerstone ceremonies?
choices: They owned all the land in the city
Their fraternity took its symbols from builders

check.why: The reading says it made sense for Masons to lead these events because their symbols came from builders.

lessons.title: Was the Revolution a Masonic Plan?
lessons.mainIdea: Masons fought on both sides of the Revolution, so the war cannot be called a Masonic plan.
reading: Some books and videos claim the American Revolution was planned inside Masonic lodges. It is a popular story, and it can sound convincing. Let's test that claim with what we know from the records.

First, Masons were on both sides. The British army had its own lodges that traveled with its regiments. Many British officers were Masons. In Boston, Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were made Masons in a lodge attached to a British regiment. Lodge histories give the date as 1775; a 2026 study argues for 1778.

Second, many key founders were not Masons. John Adams said so himself. Jefferson is not known to have joined. Careful counts of the 56 signers of the Declaration find proof of lodge membership for only a small number of them. Counts differ from source to source.

The claim is *unsupported*. Masons were part of colonial life, as churches and clubs were. Some patriots met in lodges. But no record shows the lodges as a body planning the war. Most Masons, like most colonists, simply took one side or the other.

words.d: describes a claim that has no good evidence behind it
a large unit of soldiers in an army

look.title: Sorting the Evidence
look.text: Fact 1: Paul Revere and Joseph Warren were patriot Masons. Fact 2: Many British officers were Masons in army lodges. Fact 3: John Adams said he was never a Mason. Fact 4: Only a small number of the 56 signers can be proved to be Masons.
look.prompt: Which facts might seem to support the claim of a Masonic plan? Which facts weaken it? What do you conclude?

choices: The British army banned all Masons

check.why: The reading says the British army had lodges that traveled with its regiments, and many officers were Masons.

check.q: Where were Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men made Masons?
choices: In the Grand Lodge of Maryland

check.why: The reading says they were made Masons in Boston in a lodge attached to a British regiment.

check.q: What is the best conclusion about the claim that Masons planned the Revolution?
choices: It is unsupported, because Masons were on both sides and many founders were not Masons
It is proved by the Capitol cornerstone
It is proved because Revere was a Mason
It is proved by John Adams's letter
check.why: The reading shows Masons on both sides and many non-Mason founders, and no record of lodges planning the war.

lessons.title: A Seal for a New Nation
lessons.mainIdea: In 1776 the first Great Seal committee, with artist Pierre Du Simitière, proposed an eye in a triangle, but Congress did not adopt it.
reading: On 4 July 1776, the same day it approved the Declaration, Congress asked three men to design a seal. A *seal* is an official design stamped on important papers to show they are real. The three were Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson.

They asked for help from Pierre Eugène Du Simitière, an artist living in Philadelphia. Franklin suggested a scene of Moses at the Red Sea. Jefferson suggested the people of Israel in the wilderness. The committee's final design mixed several ideas.

The committee's report of 20 August 1776 included an eye. It described the Eye of Providence in a glowing triangle, shining over the whole design. *Providence* means God's care and guidance. An eye like this was a common symbol of God's watchfulness in Christian art long before.

Congress set the design aside. But the eye idea stayed in the record. Of the three committee members, only Franklin was a Mason. Du Simitière has no records showing Masonic membership, so historians say he is not known to have been a Mason.

words.d: an official design stamped on important papers to show they are real
God's care and guidance over the world

look.title: The Committee's Report, 1776
look.text: The report describes the Eye of Providence inside a radiant triangle, with its glory reaching out over the shield and the figures of the design.
look.cite: Report of the first Great Seal committee, 20 August 1776, in Gaillard Hunt, The History of the Seal of the United States, Department of State, 1909 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Where was the eye placed in this first design? Does the report say anything about Masons?

check.q: Who was on the first Great Seal committee in 1776?
check.why: The reading says Congress asked Franklin, Adams and Jefferson to design a seal on 4 July 1776.

check.q: What does Providence mean?
check.why: The reading defines Providence as God's care and guidance.

check.q: Which statement about Du Simitière fits the evidence?
choices: He was Grand Master of Pennsylvania
He is not known to have been a Mason
check.why: The reading says no records show Du Simitière as a Mason, so historians say he is not known to have been one.

lessons.title: The Pyramid Arrives, 1782
lessons.mainIdea: The pyramid under the eye was added in 1782, when Congress finally adopted the Great Seal.
reading: After the first design was set aside, Congress tried again. A second committee worked in 1780. A third worked in 1782. Each committee added ideas. None of them finished the job alone.

In June 1782, Charles Thomson, the secretary of Congress, took the best ideas from all three. A young Philadelphia lawyer, William Barton, helped with the back of the seal. Congress adopted the Great Seal on 20 June 1782.

The front shows the eagle. The back, called the *reverse*, shows an unfinished pyramid. At its base are the Roman numerals MDCCLXXVI, which mean 1776. Above it is the eye in a triangle. There are two Latin mottos. A *motto* is a short saying. One means that God has favored our undertakings. The other means a new order of the ages.

What did the unfinished pyramid mean? The designers explained it as strength and lasting power, with the country still being built. The eye showed Providence watching over it. The record shows no Masonic plan behind these choices.

words.d: the back side of a seal, coin or medal
a short saying that states a group's goal or belief

look.title: The Seal's Long Road
rows: State Department history of the seal
look.cite: Gaillard Hunt, The History of the Seal of the United States, 1909; National Archives, Great Seal of the United States
look.prompt: How many years passed between adopting the seal and putting it on the dollar? What does that gap tell you about who designed the eye?

check.q: When did Congress adopt the Great Seal?
check.why: The reading says Congress adopted the Great Seal on 20 June 1782.

check.q: What do the Roman numerals MDCCLXXVI at the base of the pyramid mean?
check.why: The reading says MDCCLXXVI means 1776, the year of independence.

check.q: What is the reverse of a seal?
check.why: The reading defines the reverse as the back side of a seal, which shows the pyramid and the eye.

lessons.title: Onto the Dollar, 1935
lessons.mainIdea: The seal's eye and pyramid first went on the one-dollar bill in 1935, chosen by two men who were Masons.
reading: For more than 150 years, few Americans ever saw the back of the Great Seal. Then, in the 1930s, Henry A. Wallace read the State Department's history of the seal. Wallace was the Secretary of Agriculture. He took the idea to President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Roosevelt liked it. In 1935, both sides of the Great Seal were printed on the back of the one-dollar bill. That is the design Maya was holding. It is still there today, on every one-dollar bill printed since.

Here is an interesting detail. Wallace and Roosevelt were both Masons. Years later, Wallace wrote that the eye had caught their attention because Masons also used an all-seeing eye as a symbol of God. So Masons did help choose to put the seal on the dollar.

But look closely at the *timeline*. The eye was proposed in 1776 and the pyramid adopted in 1782. Wallace and Roosevelt copied a design that already existed. They did not create it. Two different questions have two different answers.

words.d: a list of events in the order they happened
the member of the president's cabinet in charge of farming

look.title: Wallace Remembers, 1951
look.text: Wallace recalls that when Roosevelt saw a picture of the seal, the all-seeing eye stood out to him, because Masons use it as a symbol of God. Wallace notes that he and Roosevelt were both Masons, and that Roosevelt then asked to put the seal on the dollar bill.
look.cite: Henry A. Wallace, letter of 1951 describing the 1935 dollar, as transcribed at greatseal.com (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Does this letter show that Masons designed the seal, or that Masons chose to put it on the dollar? Explain the difference.

check.q: When did the eye and pyramid first appear on the one-dollar bill?
check.why: The reading says both sides of the seal were printed on the one-dollar bill in 1935.

check.q: Who brought the idea of the seal on the dollar to President Roosevelt?
check.why: The reading says Wallace, the Secretary of Agriculture, read the seal's history and took the idea to Roosevelt.

check.q: Which statement fits the timeline best?
choices: Masons chose to put an existing seal on the dollar; they did not design it
check.why: The eye dates to 1776 and the pyramid to 1782; Wallace and Roosevelt only put the existing design on the dollar in 1935.

lessons.title: Testing a Claim with the Paper Trail
lessons.mainIdea: A popular claim can be tested by asking who did it, when, and what records prove it.
reading: Let's go back to Maya's question: did the Freemasons put the eye on the pyramid? Historians test a claim by following the *paper trail*, the records made at the time, step by step.

Step one: who designed the eye? The 1776 committee and its artist, Du Simitière, who is not known to have been a Mason. Step two: who added the pyramid? Thomson and Barton in 1782. The records do not show a Masonic plan. Step three: who put it on the dollar? Wallace and Roosevelt in 1935, both Masons.

There is one more twist. Masons did use an all-seeing eye in their own art. It became common in American Masonic books by the late 1790s, after the seal was adopted. Historians still debate whether Masons used it earlier. Both the seal and the lodges drew on the older Christian symbol.

So the claim is partly true and partly false. Masons did not design the seal. Two Masons did choose to put it on the dollar. A good *conclusion* keeps both facts. It does not stretch one of them into a secret plot.

words.d: the records made at the time that show step by step what happened
a decision you reach after weighing the evidence

But in 1935, two Masons, Wallace and Roosevelt, chose to put the seal on the dollar. So my cousin is partly right and partly wrong.
look.prompt: Is Maya's answer fair to both sides? What source from this chapter would you add to make it stronger?

check.why: The paper trail shows non-Masonic design in 1776 and 1782, and a choice by two Masons in 1935.
